sources.title: Western Highveld Soil fertility, NIR and MIR spectral data
sources.version: Zenodo record 17510653; version and raw file metadata to be pinned on acquisition
sources.license_status: 2026 Data in Brief article is CC BY 4.0; third-party catalog reports the Zenodo dataset as CC-BY-4.0; verify exact record/file license before redistribution.
sources.permitted_research_use: Regional South African soil-property baseline and NIR/MIR pedometric transfer evaluation after raw file, methods, sample identifiers and license are audited; not a biochar-effect-label source.
limitations: The Data in Brief paper reports 790 retained composite topsoil samples. Its methods state that 13 samples with flat/blank MIR spectra were excluded; a third-party dataset catalogue reports 803 samples. The 803-to-790 difference is consistent with those exclusions, but the exact Zenodo CSV must be inspected to determine whether it contains the pre-exclusion or retained set.
The data are composite topsoil samples from commercial cultivated grain fields, sampled in winter 2020; they are not natural soil profiles, archaeological ADE samples, or biochar-treated trials.
Reference chemistry includes pH (KCl), Bray-1 phosphorus and exchangeable K, Ca, Mg and Na; paired spectra include handheld NIR and benchtop MIR.
Coordinates were released for only a subset of samples, so complete geographic or site-held-out validation may not be possible.
The dataset has no biochar treatment/comparator labels and cannot estimate a biochar treatment effect.

sources.title: Effect of Biochar on Soil Shrinkage and Cracks and Its Evolution Under Dry and Wet Cycles: A Meta-Analysis
sources.license_status: Open-access MDPI article; confirm exact CC BY version and supplementary-data terms before redistribution.
sources.permitted_research_use: Crack-morphology and wet-dry-history evidence stratum for research synthesis after full article, extraction table and source-study crosswalk audit; not a field rate recommendation or hydraulic-transport label.
limitations: The article reports 278 paired observations extracted from 44 peer-reviewed articles and uses article-clustered robust variance estimation; paired observations must not be counted as independent articles or treatment assignments.

Article reports pooled average reductions of 39.12% in crack intensity factor and 35.17% in mean crack width; the 22.20% crack-length-density reduction was not statistically significant under article-clustered inference.
Heterogeneity exceeded 98% across the three crack metrics and all article-clustered prediction intervals crossed zero; pooled averages do not imply uniform effects or transport to a new soil domain.

Evidence for crack metrics beyond six drying-wetting cycles is sparse; the article explicitly treats later-cycle patterns as unresolved rather than establishing universal deterioration or persistence.
Application-rate subgroups differed, but application rate explained only about 12.60-15.80% of observed variation; high-rate laboratory subgroup results are not field recommendations.

The study's mechanistic interpretation of interfaces and pore restructuring is inferred from response patterns and literature, not direct observation in the meta-analysis; no raw micro-CT or field transport ground truth is supplied by this record.
No extracted effect-size table or local article file, publisher checksum or SHA-256 has been acquired.
